brief.summary: A free consumer app used by millions of curious people to explore the Moon's surface in three dimensions, with every named crater, landing site and recent mission finding placed where it actually is.
brief.user: Jolene Park, a high-school guidance counselor with no science background who opens the app a few times a year when space news catches her eye.
brief.moment: She just read a news story that a robotic lander near the lunar south pole confirmed water ice in the floor of a permanently shadowed crater, and the article named it but gave no picture of where it is. She has opened the app wanting to find the crater, see how close the lander came to it, understand why that part of the Moon never gets sunlight, and compare where it is to where Apollo 11 landed, which she remembers from school. She may also want to save the spot to show her nephew this weekend.
brief.data: About 9,000 named lunar features, each with a name, type (crater, mare, mountain, rille), latitude and longitude, diameter in km, depth, age estimate, and who it is named after. 6 Apollo landing sites with dates, crew and what was left behind; 24 robotic landers and impactors from 1959 to 2026 with operator country, landing date and status (active, ended, crashed). South-pole features: Shackleton (21 km wide, 4.2 km deep), de Gerlache, Haworth, Faustini and others, each with share of floor in permanent shadow and minimum temperature (around 40 K). The new finding: lander 'Polar Scout' landed 2026-10-28, 2.8 km from the rim of Haworth crater, reporting ice at an estimated 3–5% by weight in the regolith. Sun-angle data for any date, and the reader's 2 saved places.

prompt:
I need the front end for Lunaview. A free consumer app used by millions of curious people to explore the Moon's surface in three dimensions, with every named crater, landing site and recent mission finding placed where it actually is.

Who's using it: Jolene Park, a high-school guidance counselor with no science background who opens the app a few times a year when space news catches her eye.

What they're doing right now: She just read a news story that a robotic lander near the lunar south pole confirmed water ice in the floor of a permanently shadowed crater, and the article named it but gave no picture of where it is. She has opened the app wanting to find the crater, see how close the lander came to it, understand why that part of the Moon never gets sunlight, and compare where it is to where Apollo 11 landed, which she remembers from school. She may also want to save the spot to show her nephew this weekend.

What's in the system at this point: About 9,000 named lunar features, each with a name, type (crater, mare, mountain, rille), latitude and longitude, diameter in km, depth, age estimate, and who it is named after. 6 Apollo landing sites with dates, crew and what was left behind; 24 robotic landers and impactors from 1959 to 2026 with operator country, landing date and status (active, ended, crashed). South-pole features: Shackleton (21 km wide, 4.2 km deep), de Gerlache, Haworth, Faustini and others, each with share of floor in permanent shadow and minimum temperature (around 40 K). The new finding: lander 'Polar Scout' landed 2026-10-28, 2.8 km from the rim of Haworth crater, reporting ice at an estimated 3–5% by weight in the regolith. Sun-angle data for any date, and the reader's 2 saved places.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
